phrases.translation: Alif-Lãm-Mĩm
phrases.explanation: The chapter opens with the disconnected letters Alif-Lam-Mim. The commentary says their meaning was already explained in earlier passages and does not repeat the discussion. They introduce a chapter centered on the wise Book, gratitude, Luqman's counsel, and Allah's creative power. As with other openings of this kind, the mysterious letters give way to clear instruction and signs.

phrases.translation: These are the verses of the Book, rich in wisdom
phrases.explanation: These are the verses of the Book rich in wisdom. The commentary calls it the wise Book and says its verses are clarification and exposition. The description is not merely about beautiful speech but about guidance that makes truth clear. The chapter begins by identifying the Quran as a source of wisdom before describing the people who benefit from it.

phrases.translation: ˹It is˺ a guide and mercy for the good-doers
phrases.explanation: The Book is a guide and mercy for the good-doers. The commentary says it clarifies the truth and becomes a mercy from Allah for those who follow it and act according to it. Good-doers are those who do what Allah commands and avoid what He forbids. Guidance and mercy are therefore not abstract gifts but are experienced through obedient response.

phrases.translation: those who establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and have sure faith in the Hereafter
phrases.explanation: The good-doers establish prayer, give alms, and have certainty in the Hereafter. The commentary says they maintain the prescribed prayer with its limits, pay the obligatory alms from their wealth, and act while certain of Allah's reward and requital in the next life. These three marks join worship, social duty, and accountability. Their conduct in this world is shaped by confidence in the world to come.

phrases.translation: It is they who are ˹truly˺ guided by their Lord
phrases.explanation: Such people are truly guided by their Lord. The commentary says they stand upon a clear exposition and light from Allah, not merely on inherited opinion or personal preference. Their guidance comes from the Lord who sent the Book they follow. The phrase identifies the source of their direction before stating their outcome.

phrases.translation: and it is they who will be successful
phrases.explanation: They are also the successful. The commentary explains success as attaining what they hoped for and desired of their Lord's reward on the Day of Resurrection. Their efforts are not wasted, because the guidance they followed leads to the promised end. The verse therefore joins right direction in this life with fulfillment in the next.

phrases.translation: But there are some who employ theatrics, only to lead others away from Allah’s Way—without any knowledge—and to make a mockery of it
phrases.explanation: Some people use idle or theatrical speech to lead others away from Allah's Way without knowledge and to mock it. The commentary records many interpretations of the idle talk, including singing, buying singing-girls, drums, idolatry, or any speech that diverts from Allah's path. It prefers a general meaning: anything whose hearing turns people away from Quran recitation, remembrance, and obedience. Their aim is not innocent entertainment but diversion and ridicule.

phrases.translation: They will suffer a humiliating punishment
phrases.explanation: They will suffer a humiliating punishment. The commentary says this is a disgracing punishment in the Fire on the Day of Resurrection. The penalty corresponds to the arrogance and mockery with which they treated guidance. What they used to belittle the path of Allah becomes the cause of their own humiliation before Him.

phrases.translation: Whenever Our revelations are recited to them, they turn away in arrogance as if they did not hear them
phrases.explanation: When Allah's revelations are recited to such people, they turn away in arrogance as though they had not heard them. The commentary says they turn away from the truth with great haughtiness and refuse to listen or respond. Their physical hearing is intact, but pride makes them behave as if the words never reached them. The rejection is therefore deliberate, not accidental.

phrases.translation: as if there is deafness in their ears. So give them good news ˹O Prophet˺ of a painful punishment
phrases.explanation: They act as though heaviness or deafness fills their ears, and the Prophet is told to give them good news of painful punishment. The commentary explains the deafness as a weight that prevents true hearing. The phrase good news is used ironically, since the announcement is of Allah's painful punishment in the Fire. Their contempt for revelation is answered by a message they will not be able to dismiss.

phrases.translation: Surely those who believe and do good will have the Gardens of Bliss
phrases.explanation: Those who believe and do good will have the Gardens of Bliss. The commentary says they believe in Allah's oneness, affirm His Messenger, follow him, obey Allah's commands, and avoid His prohibitions. Their faith is joined to action, and their action is shaped by revelation. The Gardens are not presented as a reward for words alone but for a life of obedient faith.

phrases.translation: staying there forever. Allah’s promise is true
phrases.explanation: They will stay in the Gardens forever, and Allah's promise is true. The commentary says their stay has no end and that Allah's promise contains no doubt and will not be broken. The permanence of the reward is grounded in the truthfulness of the One who promised it. The verse therefore gives believers confidence that what they hope for is secure.

phrases.translation: And He is the Almighty, All-Wise
phrases.explanation: Allah is Almighty and All-Wise. The commentary says His might appears in severe retribution against those who associate partners with Him and turn away from His path, while His wisdom appears in His governance of creation. The same verse that promises mercy to believers also warns opponents. Power and wisdom ensure that both the promise and the warning are fulfilled.

phrases.translation: He created the heavens without pillars—as you can see—and placed firm mountains upon the earth so it does not shake with you
phrases.explanation: Allah created the heavens without visible pillars and placed firm mountains on the earth so it does not shake with people. The commentary notes that some interpreters say the heavens have pillars that cannot be seen, while others say they have none. It also says the mountains stabilize the earth so creatures can live on it. The visible order of the world is presented as part of Allah's wisdom and care.

phrases.translation: and scattered throughout it all types of creatures
phrases.explanation: Allah scattered every type of creature throughout the earth. The commentary explains this as dispersing all kinds of animals across its surface, with the word understood either as all that crawls or all that eats and drinks. The variety of living beings is not accidental but part of His creation. The phrase moves from the stability of the earth to the abundance of life upon it.

phrases.translation: And We send down rain from the sky, causing every type of fine plant to grow on earth
phrases.explanation: Allah sends rain from the sky and causes every kind of fine plant to grow. The commentary says the rain brings forth every pair or kind of plant with fair and noble growth. Water from above becomes the means of beauty and sustenance below. Together with mountains, animals, and heavens, this growth displays a world dependent on divine provision.

phrases.translation: This is Allah’s creation. Now show Me what those ˹gods˺ other than Him have created
phrases.explanation: Allah points to what He has created and challenges people to show what other gods have made. The commentary says the heavens, earth, animals, and plants all belong to His creative act, so the idols have no comparable work that would give them a claim to worship. The challenge is direct and public. Creation itself becomes the evidence for exclusive worship.

phrases.translation: In fact, the wrongdoers are clearly astray
phrases.explanation: The wrongdoers are clearly astray. The commentary says they do not worship idols because those objects create anything, but because they have deviated from the path of truth. Their error is manifest to anyone who reflects on it. The verse therefore treats idolatry as a visible failure to recognize the Creator's unique work.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We blessed Luqmân with wisdom, ˹saying˺, “Be grateful to Allah, for whoever is grateful, it is only for their own good
phrases.explanation: Allah gave Luqman wisdom, and the first content of that wisdom is gratitude to Allah. The commentary explains wisdom as understanding in religion, intelligence, and correctness in speech, without prophethood, though it notes a report that he was a prophet. It also preserves traditions about his humble social origin. His example shows that wisdom is a divine gift rather than a matter of status, and gratitude is its proper expression.

phrases.translation: And whoever is ungrateful, then surely Allah is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy
phrases.explanation: Whoever is grateful benefits only themselves, while Allah remains Self-Sufficient and Praiseworthy. The commentary says gratitude brings abundant reward and saves a person from ruin, but ingratitude harms only the ungrateful. Allah's dominion is not increased by thanks or diminished by denial, and He is praised in every state. The verse therefore makes thankfulness a human need rather than a divine need.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when Luqmân said to his son, while advising him, “O my dear son
phrases.explanation: Allah tells the Prophet to remember Luqman's tender admonition to his son. The phrase O my dear son shows affection within correction, and the commentary frames the scene as an exhortation. Wisdom is therefore passed on through personal counsel, not abstract teaching alone. The father's love gives weight to the warning that follows.

phrases.translation: Never associate ˹anything˺ with Allah ˹in worship˺, for associating ˹others with Him˺ is truly the worst of all wrongs
phrases.explanation: Luqman tells his son never to associate anything with Allah in worship, because idolatry is the worst of wrongs. The commentary calls it a tremendous error in statement, since it gives the Creator's right to something that is not divine. The warning stands at the head of Luqman's advice. Before commands about prayer or conduct, the son is taught to guard the oneness of Allah.

phrases.translation: And We have commanded people to ˹honour˺ their parents. Their mothers bore them through hardship upon hardship
phrases.explanation: Allah commands people to honor their parents, especially reminding them of their mothers' hardship. The commentary explains hardship upon hardship as repeated weakness during pregnancy, exertion upon exertion, or the child's frailty added to the mother's weakness. Reports connect the passage to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and his mother. The command to honor parents is grounded in the real suffering involved in bringing a child into the world.

phrases.translation: and their weaning takes two years. So be grateful to Me and your parents. To Me is the final return
phrases.explanation: Weaning takes two years, so people should be grateful to Allah and their parents, and to Allah is the final return. The commentary says gratitude is owed to Allah for His favors and to parents for raising the child through fatigue and hardship. Allah will question people about that gratitude and their goodness to parents. The family relationship is therefore placed under divine accountability.

phrases.translation: But if they pressure you to associate with Me what you have no knowledge of, do not obey them
phrases.explanation: If parents pressure a person to associate partners with Allah, they must not be obeyed in that demand. The commentary says there is no knowledge that Allah has a partner, so the pressure calls to something false. This verse continues the same boundary found earlier in the Quran. Family ties are honored, but they do not extend to obeying a command that contradicts the Creator's right.

phrases.translation: Still keep their company in this world courteously, and follow the way of those who turn to Me ˹in devotion˺
phrases.explanation: Even then, parents must be treated with kindness in worldly life, and the way of those who turn to Allah must be followed. The commentary says to obey parents in matters that involve no sin, while following the path of those who abandoned idolatry, returned to Islam, and followed Muhammad. Refusing religious compliance does not permit harshness. Obedience to Allah and courteous family conduct are held together.

phrases.translation: Then to Me you will ˹all˺ return, and then I will inform you of what you used to do
phrases.explanation: All people will return to Allah, and He will inform them of what they used to do. The commentary says this includes both good and evil deeds, followed by fitting requital. The statement is inserted within Luqman's exhortation to remind the listener that parental pressure and family bonds do not cancel accountability. Every choice remains before Allah, who knows and repays it.

phrases.translation: ˹Luqmân added,˺ “O my dear son! ˹Even˺ if a deed were the weight of a mustard seed—be it ˹hidden˺ in a rock or in the heavens or the earth—Allah will bring it forth
phrases.explanation: Luqman tells his son that even a deed the weight of a mustard seed will be brought forth by Allah. The commentary explains that this applies to both good and evil deeds, even if hidden in a rock, a mountain, the heavens, or the earth. It records different interpretations of the rock, including the foundation rock of the earth or mountains, and says Allah will bring the deed forth for full recompense on the Day of Resurrection.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah is Most Subtle, All-Aware
phrases.explanation: Allah is Most Subtle and All-Aware. The commentary says He is subtle in extracting the smallest deed from wherever it lies and fully knows its place. Nothing hidden by size or location escapes His knowledge. The phrase assures the listener that moral reality cannot be lost in the vastness of creation.

phrases.translation: O my dear son! Establish prayer, encourage what is good and forbid what is evil
phrases.explanation: Luqman tells his son to establish prayer, encourage what is good, and forbid what is evil. The commentary explains prayer as observing its prescribed limits, encouraging good as calling people to obey Allah, and forbidding evil as warning against disobedience and forbidden acts. The counsel moves from personal worship to responsibility for the moral life of the community.

phrases.translation: and endure patiently whatever befalls you. Surely this is a resolve to aspire to
phrases.explanation: He also tells him to endure patiently whatever befalls him, for this is a resolve to aspire to. The commentary says the patience especially concerns harm from people when one commands good and forbids evil. Such harm must not turn a person away from the task. The phrase calls this steadfastness one of the matters firmly commanded by Allah.

phrases.translation: And do not turn your nose up to people, nor walk pridefully upon the earth
phrases.explanation: Luqman tells his son not to turn his face away from people or walk pridefully on the earth. The commentary explains the first command as refusing to look at someone because of arrogance or disdain. It records related interpretations about turning away from someone out of rancor or twisting the mouth in affected speech. The second command forbids walking with haughtiness. Both address pride expressed in the body.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah does not like whoever is arrogant, boastful
phrases.explanation: Allah does not like the arrogant boaster. The commentary says the conceited person exalts himself above others, while the boaster enumerates what Allah has given him without thanking Allah. The problem is not possessing blessings but treating them as grounds for superiority. The verse therefore traces social arrogance to forgetfulness of the Giver.

phrases.translation: Be moderate in your pace
phrases.explanation: Luqman says to be moderate in one's pace. The commentary explains this as humility in walking, with no arrogance and no excessive haste, but a deliberate gait. The command follows the previous warning about pride, showing that inward attitude should shape ordinary movement. Even the way a person walks can reveal either humility or self-importance.

phrases.translation: And lower your voice, for the ugliest of all voices is certainly the braying of donkeys
phrases.explanation: He also says to lower the voice, because the ugliest of voices is the braying of donkeys. The commentary explains this as moderation in speech and notes that the donkey's voice is described as harsh and repugnant. If raising the voice were good, it would not have been attributed to donkeys. The command therefore joins modest movement with restraint in speech.

phrases.translation: Have you not seen that Allah has subjected for you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth
phrases.explanation: Allah has subjected whatever is in the heavens and on the earth to human benefit. The commentary lists the sun, moon, stars, clouds, animals, trees, water, seas, ships, and other benefits, all serving human nourishment, provision, sustenance, and pleasure. The world is not presented as hostile or meaningless but as arranged for human use. This subjection should produce gratitude and recognition of the Creator.

phrases.translation: and has lavished His favours upon you, both seen and unseen
phrases.explanation: Allah has lavished His favors on people, both seen and unseen. The commentary notes accepted readings in the singular and plural. The singular is interpreted as Islam or the testimony that there is no god but Allah, while the plural refers to all the favors just mentioned. Visible favors appear in words and deeds, hidden favors in conviction and knowledge of the heart. Both kinds come from Him.

phrases.translation: ˹Still˺ there are some who dispute about Allah without knowledge, or guidance, or an enlightening scripture
phrases.explanation: Yet some people dispute about Allah without knowledge, guidance, or an enlightening scripture. The commentary says they argue about His oneness and exclusive worship without knowing what they claim, without clear exposition, and without revelation to support them. Their dispute has neither reason nor revelation behind it. The verse contrasts abundant divine favors with baseless argument.

phrases.translation: When it is said to them, “Follow what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “No! We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing
phrases.explanation: When people are told to follow what Allah revealed, they answer that they will follow only what their forefathers practiced. The commentary says they claim their ancestors were upon truth and prefer inherited religion to the revelation that distinguishes truth from falsehood. Their answer replaces divine guidance with custom. The verse exposes how ancestry can be used to avoid a present call to truth.

phrases.translation: ˹Would they still do so˺ even if Satan is inviting them to the torment of the Blaze
phrases.explanation: The question asks whether they would still follow that way if Satan were calling them to the punishment of the Blaze. The commentary says Satan beautifies their evil deeds, misguidance, disbelief, and refusal to follow Allah's Book, thereby summoning them to a blazing Fire. Ancestral practice is no defense when its outcome is ruin. The verse reveals the destructive power behind apparently respectable tradition.

phrases.translation: Whoever fully submits themselves to Allah and is a good-doer, they have certainly grasped the firmest hand-hold
phrases.explanation: Whoever submits fully to Allah and does good has grasped the firmest hand-hold. The commentary explains submission as humbling oneself in servitude and acknowledging Allah's divinity, while doing good means obeying His commands and prohibitions. The hand-hold is a parable for what cannot break and protects from punishment. A report also connects it to the testimony that there is no god but Allah.

phrases.translation: And with Allah rests the outcome of ˹all˺ affairs
phrases.explanation: With Allah rests the outcome of all affairs. The commentary says every matter, good or evil, returns to Him, and He questions people about it and repays them accordingly. Human choices do not disappear into history. Their final outcome lies with the One who judges and requites them.

phrases.translation: But whoever disbelieves, do not let their disbelief grieve you ˹O Prophet˺
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told not to let the disbelief of those who reject Allah grieve him. The commentary says he should not consume himself with regret over them, because their final destination is to Allah. This does not make their disbelief insignificant, but it places judgment where it belongs. The command consoles the messenger without denying the seriousness of rejection.

phrases.translation: To Us is their return, and We will inform them of all they did. Surely Allah knows best what is ˹hidden˺ in the heart
phrases.explanation: They will return to Allah, who will inform them of what they did, and He knows what is hidden in the heart. The commentary says their contemptible deeds will be made known and requited, and Allah knows the disbelief and preference for obedience to Satan concealed in their breasts. Nothing internal escapes His knowledge. Judgment therefore reaches both outward actions and inward allegiance.

phrases.translation: We allow them enjoyment for a little while
phrases.explanation: Allah allows the disbelievers enjoyment for a little while. The commentary says this is a brief respite in the worldly life, during which they take pleasure in what they have been given. The enjoyment is real but temporary. It should not be mistaken for final success or safety from judgment.

phrases.translation: then ˹in time˺ We will force them into a harsh torment
phrases.explanation: Then Allah will drive them into a harsh torment. The commentary says they will be forced unwillingly to a severe punishment, identified as the punishment of the Fire. The movement from brief pleasure to severe chastisement is certain. The verse therefore warns that delay does not cancel the outcome.

phrases.translation: And if you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will definitely say, “Allah
phrases.explanation: If the polytheists are asked who created the heavens and earth, they say Allah. The commentary emphasizes that they acknowledge Him as Creator despite associating partners with Him. Their own answer undermines their worship of beings that create nothing. The verse begins with a confession they already make.

phrases.translation: Say, “Praise be to Allah!” In fact, most of them do not know
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to say all praise belongs to Allah, though most people do not know. The commentary says praise belongs to the One who created, not to objects that create nothing and are themselves created. Most of the polytheists do not know where praise and gratitude truly belong. Their knowledge of creation should have led them to exclusive worship.

phrases.translation: To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth
phrases.explanation: Everything in the heavens and earth belongs to Allah. The commentary says this includes idols and carved images, whether worshipped or not, because all are His possession. Nothing exists outside His ownership. The verse therefore removes any basis for treating created objects as independent powers.

phrases.translation: Allah is truly the Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy
phrases.explanation: Allah is Self-Sufficient and Praiseworthy. The commentary says He has no need of idolaters, of any servant, or of creation as a whole, while all creatures need Him. He is praised for the blessings He has bestowed on creation. The phrase joins independence with worthiness of praise, showing that worship benefits the worshipper rather than Allah.

phrases.translation: If all the trees on earth were pens and the ocean ˹were ink˺, refilled by seven other oceans
phrases.explanation: If all trees on earth were pens and the ocean were ink with seven more seas to replenish it, Allah's words would still not be exhausted. The commentary says the pens would break and the ink would run out before His words, wisdom, knowledge, and creative wonders were finished. Reports connect the verse to disputes with Jewish scholars about the Torah and the little knowledge given to people. The image answers any claim that divine knowledge can be contained.

phrases.translation: the Words of Allah would not be exhausted. Surely Allah is Almighty, All-Wise
phrases.explanation: Allah is Almighty and All-Wise. The commentary explains His might as power to punish those who associate partners with Him or call on another god, and His wisdom as His governance of creation. The verse about inexhaustible words ends by grounding that abundance in divine power and wisdom. Human knowledge remains limited, but Allah's command and knowledge do not run out.

phrases.translation: The creation and resurrection of you ˹all˺ is as simple ˹for Him˺ as that of a single soul
phrases.explanation: Creating and resurrecting all people is as simple for Allah as creating and resurrecting a single soul. The commentary says nothing He wills is impossible or withheld from Him, since His command is Be and it is. Few and many are equal before that command. The verse therefore answers denial of resurrection by pointing to the ease of divine creation.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing
phrases.explanation: Allah is All-Hearing and All-Seeing. The commentary says He hears what the polytheists say and fabricate about Him, including claims that He has partners, and sees all deeds. He will repay people with the requital they deserve. The names therefore connect His power to create with His complete awareness of human speech and action.

phrases.translation: Do you not see that Allah causes the night to merge into the day and the day into the night
phrases.explanation: Allah causes the night to merge into the day and the day into the night. The commentary explains this as the shortening of one being added to the lengthening of the other through the hours of the year. The regular alteration of darkness and light is not independent but governed by Allah. It is presented as a visible proof against those who do not recognize His greatness.

phrases.translation: and has subjected the sun and the moon, each orbiting for an appointed term, and that Allah is All-Aware of what you do
phrases.explanation: He has subjected the sun and moon, each running for an appointed term, and He is aware of what people do. The commentary says they move by His command for the benefit of creation until a known limit, when they will be rolled up. Allah knows every good and evil deed and will repay it. Though the Prophet is addressed, the warning is aimed at the polytheists who ignore these signs.

phrases.translation: That is because Allah ˹alone˺ is the Truth and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood
phrases.explanation: Allah alone is the Truth, and what people invoke besides Him is falsehood. The commentary says the signs just mentioned, such as the merging of night and day, are accomplished by the One who is truly God. The objects worshipped beside Him are false and perishing, unable to do any of these acts. Divinity belongs to the One whose power produces the order of the world.

phrases.translation: and ˹because˺ Allah ˹alone˺ is the Most High, All-Great
phrases.explanation: Allah alone is the Most High and All-Great. The commentary explains that He is exalted above all things, and everything beneath Him is submissive and obedient before His greatness. The verse therefore connects the previous signs to His unique rank. Because He alone is high and great, no created object can share His worship.

phrases.translation: Do you not see that the ships sail ˹smoothly˺ through the sea by the grace of Allah so that He may show you some of His signs
phrases.explanation: Ships sail through the sea by Allah's grace so that He may show people some of His signs. The commentary says their movement is a favor to His creatures and a proof against them. The sea, which can overwhelm human beings, is made passable under Allah's order. What appears as ordinary travel becomes an indication that Allah is the Truth.

phrases.translation: Surely in this are signs for whoever is steadfast, grateful
phrases.explanation: In this are signs for everyone steadfast and grateful. The commentary explains the steadfast person as one who restrains himself from what Allah has forbidden, and the grateful person as one who thanks Him for His favors. Patience and gratitude are described as deeds of people of intellect and reason. Such people are able to perceive the signs that others overlook.

phrases.translation: And as soon as they are overwhelmed by waves like mountains, they cry out to Allah ˹alone˺ in sincere devotion
phrases.explanation: When waves like mountains overwhelm people at sea, they cry out to Allah alone in sincere devotion. The commentary says the waves are like dark, overshadowing banks of water, and those who normally worship idols flee to Allah when they fear drowning. In that moment they devote obedience purely to Him, call on no partner, and seek help from no other. Danger strips away their false worship.

phrases.translation: But when He delivers them ˹safely˺ to shore, only some become relatively grateful
phrases.explanation: When Allah delivers them safely to land, only some become relatively grateful. The commentary explains the word for some as those who are moderate. It records interpretations that they are moderate in speech while still concealing disbelief, or that they occupy a middle state in righteousness. The phrase suggests that deliverance does not produce full gratitude in most. Their earlier sincerity fades with safety.

phrases.translation: And none rejects Our signs except whoever is deceitful, ungrateful
phrases.explanation: None reject Allah's signs except the deceitful and ungrateful. The commentary explains the deceitful one as a betrayer of covenants, with treachery described as among the ugliest forms of betrayal, and the ungrateful one as someone who denies favors and does not thank Allah for bounty. Rejecting signs is therefore joined to betrayal. It is not honest doubt but a violation of trust.

phrases.translation: O humanity! Be mindful of your Lord, and beware of a Day when no parent will be of any benefit to their child
phrases.explanation: Humanity is told to be mindful of its Lord and beware of a Day when no parent will benefit a child. The commentary says on that Day the affair belongs to the One who cannot be overcome, and no intercession or means will help except the good deeds a person sent ahead in worldly life. Family ties, however strong, cannot replace personal obedience. The warning calls for preparation before the Day arrives.

phrases.translation: nor will a child be of any benefit to their parent. Surely Allah’s promise is true
phrases.explanation: Nor will a child benefit a parent, and Allah's promise is true. The commentary says the coming of the Day is certain because Allah has promised it and does not break His word. The second half of the phrase removes any hope that another family member can carry one's burden. Each person stands before Allah with what they themselves have done.

phrases.translation: So do not let the life of this world deceive you, nor let the Chief Deceiver deceive you about Allah
phrases.explanation: People are told not to let worldly life or the Chief Deceiver deceive them about Allah. The commentary explains worldly adornment and pleasure as distractions from preparing for that Day. The deceiver is often identified with Satan, but the word can include any person, thing, or worldly life that misleads. One report describes deception as sinning while still expecting forgiveness. The verse warns against both worldly distraction and false confidence in Allah.

phrases.translation: Indeed, Allah ˹alone˺ has the knowledge of the Hour
phrases.explanation: Allah alone has knowledge of the Hour. The commentary says no one knows when the Resurrection will come, in what year, month, night, or day, and it will arrive suddenly. Reports connect the verse to questions about the Hour, rain, the womb, and death, and identify these matters as keys of the unseen reserved for Allah. The command to fear the Day is therefore grounded in its unknown timing.

phrases.translation: He sends down the rain, and knows what is in the wombs. No soul knows what it will earn for tomorrow
phrases.explanation: Allah sends down rain, knows what is in the wombs, and no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow. The commentary says no one else can send the rain, and no one knows what the womb contains, whether male or female, or what a person will do of good or evil on the next day. These realities surround human life yet remain beyond human control. The verse uses ordinary uncertainty to point to divine knowledge.

phrases.translation: and no soul knows in what land it will die. Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware
phrases.explanation: No soul knows in what land it will die, and Allah is All-Knowing and All-Aware. The commentary says no person knows whether death will come on sea or land, in a plain or in the mountains, while Allah knows all things, hidden and manifest. The chapter ends by placing the future entirely within His knowledge. Human beings are therefore called to live in reverent readiness rather than illusion.
